bible.world: A moonlit, layered paper city of gilded statues, tall columns, poor attic rooms, and frost-bright streets where flight, falling leaves, and tears become moving pop-up scenes. The story moves from jewel-bright admiration through sacrifice to a quiet, grey, transcendent ending.
arc: The city admires a beautiful prince who seems to possess perfect happiness.
A swallow chooses a river reed over migration and is left lonely.
Rain becomes tears, revealing the prince's sorrow and the city's hidden misery.
The prince begins sacrificing his jewels to relieve individual suffering.
The swallow gives up his journey to become the prince's messenger.
The prince surrenders his gold and sight for the poor.
Death, ruin, and divine redemption transform sacrifice into eternal praise.

cast.name: Happy Prince
cast.look: Statue gilded all over with thin leaves of fine gold, two bright sapphire eyes, a large red ruby on his sword-hilt, beautiful face, feet fastened to a pedestal, and a leaden heart inside.
cast.personality_in_motion: Regal and still, speaking in a low musical voice, turning his hidden sorrow into gentle commands.

pages.scene: The gilded prince stands motionless on his tall column while citizens below admire, criticise, and dream around him.
pages.why: This tableau establishes the prince's beauty, public meaning, and emotional distance before any sorrow appears.

pages.scene: The swallow courts the slender reed all summer, then leaves her and flies toward the city.
pages.why: The swallow's restless attachment and departure create the travelling heart that will later serve the prince.

pages.scene: The swallow settles between the prince's feet, rain falls from a clear sky, and he looks up at the weeping statue.
pages.why: The impossible rain turns the statue from ornament into a living, suffering presence.

pages.scene: The prince explains his past in Sans-Souci and the misery he can now see from his high place.
pages.why: His memory of pleasure contrasted with present suffering gives weight to every later sacrifice.

pages.scene: The prince describes the sick boy and asks for his ruby while the swallow remembers Egypt.
pages.why: The first request establishes the pattern of giving and the swallow's reluctance.

pages.scene: The swallow refuses because of rude boys, then agrees to stay one cold night and become messenger.
pages.why: The swallow's change of heart begins his transformation from traveller to helper.

pages.scene: The swallow carries the ruby to the poor house, cools the boy's forehead, and returns warm with goodness.
pages.why: The first completed gift shows how small action brings immediate relief and changes the giver.

pages.scene: The swallow bathes, is noticed by a professor, and proudly visits monuments before returning at moonrise.
pages.why: His brief celebrity and high spirits make his later renunciation more moving.

pages.scene: The prince describes the cold, hungry student and asks the swallow to take one sapphire eye.
pages.why: The request now costs the prince part of his sight, deepening the sacrifice.

pages.scene: The swallow plucks the sapphire, enters through the roof hole, and leaves the student inspired.
pages.why: The jewel becomes art and food, showing the prince's gifts enabling creation as well as survival.

pages.scene: The swallow visits the harbour, tries to leave, then hears of the barefoot match-girl and is commanded to take the last eye.
pages.why: The prince's blindness and the swallow's resistance raise the cost of compassion to its peak.

pages.scene: The swallow gives the match-girl the sapphire, she runs home laughing, and he returns to stay with the blind prince.
pages.why: The swallow's choice to remain turns charity into companionship.

pages.scene: The swallow tells stories of strange lands from the prince's shoulder, then flies over the city to report its misery.
pages.why: The reversal from marvellous travel stories to human suffering expands the prince's concern to the whole city.

pages.scene: The swallow sees rich merriment, starving children, and two boys driven from a bridge archway into the rain.
pages.why: These images justify the prince's final, most sweeping sacrifice of his gold.

pages.scene: Leaf by leaf the swallow removes the prince's gold and carries it to the poor until children laugh and play.
pages.why: The gold physically disappears while human faces grow rosier, making sacrifice visibly worthwhile.

pages.scene: Frost covers the city while the poor little swallow grows colder, eating crumbs and flapping to keep warm.
pages.why: The worsening weather makes the swallow's loyalty and the prince's bareness painfully concrete.

pages.scene: The swallow kisses the prince on the lips, dies at his feet, and the leaden heart snaps in two.
pages.why: The quiet death and cracked heart turn the story from social charity into tragedy.

pages.scene: Officials declare the shabby prince useless, pull down the statue, melt it, and quarrel over a replacement.
pages.why: The civic response exposes how society mistakes beauty and usefulness for true value.

pages.scene: The broken heart will not melt, the dead swallow lies beside it, and an angel carries both to God.
pages.why: The final image redeems ruin by naming the heart and bird the city's most precious things.
